resources.string: Local-only Android firewall inspired by enterprise packet flow.
VPN mode captures traffic metadata, applies app and DNS rules, and stores local logs on device only.
TacU-NS Firewall stores rules and logs on device only. No user account is required.
This release uses Android VpnService for local traffic handling. All firewall decisions are made on-device. No data is shared with third parties.
Monitoring traffic and enforcing local rules.
This app creates a local VPN interface to inspect traffic metadata on your device, apply app and DNS rules, and store security events.
Sentinel processes all traffic locally on your device. No browsing data is sent to external servers. Domain block rules are downloaded from open-source community lists only.

This shows how the firewall protects your phone, using three simple badges.

\"VPN Firewall\" means the app uses a private local connection on your phone to check every website you visit. \"DNS Filter\" means it checks website addresses before your phone connects to them. \"No Root\" means it works without needing special admin access to your phone.
Android requires a VPN-style connection to let an app check traffic without root access. This app only uses that connection on your own phone — your data is not sent to any outside server.
You get strong protection without rooting your phone or sending your browsing through someone else\'s servers.
Seeing a \"VPN\" icon in your status bar is normal and expected while this protection is on.
These four boxes show what your firewall has done today.

\"Threats Blocked\" counts harmful sites stopped. \"Connections\" counts normal sites allowed. \"Threat Database\" shows how many bad addresses this app knows about. \"DNS Requests\" is the total of both.
This gives you a quick, simple view of how active and how protected your phone has been today.
You can see at a glance that the app is working, without needing to check any settings.
Block any domain from Apps tab
A single number out of 100 that shows how well protected your phone is right now.
The app checks 5 things and adds up points for each one you have turned on or achieved. A higher score means better protection.
Instead of checking many settings one by one, this one number tells you your overall protection level at a glance.
You can quickly see if something important is turned off, and fix it to raise your score.
VPN Firewall Active (up to 30 points): points are earned when the firewall is turned on.
Threat Database Loaded (up to 25 points): points are earned once enough known-bad websites are loaded.
Threats Blocked Today (up to 15 points): points are earned once the app has blocked at least one threat today.
Auto-Start Enabled (up to 10 points): points are earned when \"Boot on Start\" is turned on in Settings.
Active Block Rate (up to 20 points): points are earned based on what share of today\'s traffic was blocked.
A summary of your firewall\'s activity over the last 7 days.
It shows how many threats were blocked, how many connections were allowed, and your block rate (the share of traffic that was blocked).
A single day does not always tell the full story. Looking at a week shows patterns, like which app or website keeps trying to reach you.
You can spot repeat problem apps or websites and decide if you want to block them by hand.
Tap the download icon to save this report as a text file you can keep or share.
A chart showing your firewall\'s activity hour by hour, for the last 24 hours.
Each bar is one hour. Red shows blocked threats, cyan (light blue) shows normal allowed connections.
Taller bars mean busier hours. This helps you see when your phone is most active, and when most threats were stopped.
You can notice unusual spikes, for example if a lot of threats were blocked at a time you were not even using your phone.
This shows the three layers of protection working together to keep you safe.

\"Ad & Tracker Blocking\" stops known ad and tracking websites. \"DNS Firewall\" checks every website address your phone tries to visit. \"Custom Domain Rules\" blocks any extra websites you added yourself.
Using more than one layer of protection catches more threats than relying on just one method.
Fewer ads, less tracking of your activity, and stronger protection against harmful websites.
You can add your own websites to block from the Protect tab.
A list of the newest harmful website addresses this app has stopped.
Each row shows one blocked address, how many times it was tried, and that it came from the DNS Firewall.
Seeing exactly what was blocked helps you understand what kind of threats your phone runs into.
You can confirm the app is actively protecting you and see if any app on your phone is behaving suspiciously.
A list of the apps on your phone sending the most internet requests today.
It ranks apps by how many website or server addresses they looked up today, whether allowed or blocked.
Some apps use the internet far more than others, often without you realizing it.
You can spot an app using more data or making more connections than you expect, then check or block it from the Apps tab.
A list of websites your phone visits often, that you have not blocked yet.
The app looks at your recent traffic and suggests websites you may want to block, based on how often they show up.
Some websites (like ad networks or trackers) show up again and again without you noticing. This helps you find them.
You can block a suggested website with one tap, or dismiss it if you want to keep allowing it.
Dismissing a suggestion just hides it from this list. It does not block or allow the website.
A way to block all websites that end in a specific country\'s web address, like \".ru\" or \".cn\".
Turning on a country blocks every website registered with that country\'s ending, all at once.
Some countries have a lot of scam or malware websites registered under their address ending.
One switch blocks a whole group of risky websites, instead of blocking them one at a time.
This blocks by web address ending, not by where a server physically is. A safe, well-known website using one of these endings would also be blocked.
A place to block or unblock any single website address yourself.
Type in a website address and tap Block. It will stop working on your phone until you unblock it.
Sometimes you know exactly which website you want to stop, like a distracting app\'s website or an unwanted service.
You get full, simple control over any specific website, beyond what blocklists or country blocking cover.
Type the plain address, like \"example.com\", without \"https://\" or \"www.\".
Blocking \"example.com\" also blocks every subdomain, like \"news.example.com\".
A timer that blocks certain types of websites, only during set days and hours.
Pick a category (like Social Media or Games), a time window, and which days it applies. During that window, those sites are blocked automatically.
You may want to block distracting apps only during work hours or bedtime, not all day, every day.
You get a hands-free way to build healthier habits, without having to remember to turn blocking on and off yourself.
\"FREE · 1/1\" means you can have 1 active schedule.
A way to save your block list to a file, or load one back in.
Back Up All saves your domains, app rules, schedule and blocklist choices into one file. Restore reads that file and puts everything back.
This lets you keep a backup of your settings, or move them to a new phone.
You will not lose your setup if you switch phones or reinstall the app.
You can only use export or import a limited number of times per day, to keep the app running smoothly.
Small labels on each app that show its recent network activity at a glance.
Each app card can show up to six different badges, explained below.
These badges help you spot which apps are worth a closer look, without opening each one.
You can quickly find apps that may be using more data or behaving unusually, and decide whether to block them.
Threats badge: how many harmful connections from this app were blocked in the last 7 days.
Status badge (BLOCKED / PARTIAL / ALLOWED): whether this app is fully blocked, blocked on only Wi-Fi or only Data, or fully allowed.
Rate badge (like \"12/min\"): how many website look-ups this app made per minute, recently.
SPIKE badge: this app suddenly made far more connections than usual.
BEACON badge: this app is contacting the same address again and again at steady time gaps, which can be a sign of tracking software.
UPD badge: this app\'s traffic pattern changed noticeably after its last update.
Tap Wi-Fi or Data button on any app to block it
When you block an app, the websites you blocked will open again. Activity logs also stop for your other apps. Unblock all apps to make both work again.

Tap Installed to see only the apps you installed. Tap System to see only the apps that came with your phone.
System apps rarely need to be blocked, so hiding them keeps your list short and easy to read.
Turn this on only if you need to block a specific built-in app, otherwise leave it off for a cleaner list.

QUERIES is the total number of website look-ups this app made. BLOCKED and ALLOWED show how many of those were stopped or let through. BLOCK RATE is the percentage that were blocked. Below that, you can see the specific websites this app tried to reach the most.
This helps you understand exactly what one app is doing on the internet, not just a summary.
If an app looks suspicious, you can check exactly which websites it is contacting before deciding to block it.
Block all domains by country TLD
A record of every website address your phone has tried to reach.

\"Event-based\" means the app only records which website address was contacted and whether it was blocked or allowed. \"No packet inspection\" means it does not read or store the actual content of your messages, photos, or browsing.
This gives you a clear activity history while still respecting your privacy.
You can see exactly what was blocked or allowed, with the confidence that your private content was never read or stored.
This permanently deletes your activity history on this device. It can\'t be undone.
Small labels that appear next to a blocked or allowed website in your logs.
These badges tell you quickly why a website was flagged, without needing to look it up yourself.
You can understand what kind of risk was stopped, and feel confident the app is protecting you correctly.
Threat label (like \"AD/TRACKER\"): the category of harm this website is known for.
DGA?: this website\'s address looks randomly generated by a computer, a common trick used by malware to hide.
TUNNEL?: this app may be using website look-ups to sneak data in or out, bypassing normal traffic rules.
Category badge: for allowed websites, shows what type of website it is, such as social media or ads.
A \"≈ domain.com\" badge means this address looks a lot like a well-known site you trust — it could be a scam trying to trick you into typing your password on a fake page.
Enable VPN to start capturing events
A world map showing where the websites your phone contacts are located.

The dot in the middle is your phone. Each line goes to the country of a server used by a website your apps opened today. Bigger dots mean more visits. Blocked websites are not on the map: they were stopped before any server was reached.
It gives you a simple picture of where your phone\'s internet connections go.
You can spot if your phone is unexpectedly contacting a country you do not recognize.
Big websites often use a server close to you, so the country shown is usually where the server is, not where the company is. The map only shows real activity from today.
A list of the websites blocked the most times today.
Each row shows a website and how many times it was blocked today. Blocked websites have no server location, because they were stopped before connecting.
Seeing which websites are blocked most often shows you what keeps trying to reach your phone.
You can notice if one website or tracker is unusually persistent, and decide if it needs extra attention.

Your password is never saved. Only a scrambled fingerprint of it is kept on this phone, and it is never uploaded anywhere.
Use 8 or more characters with an uppercase letter, a lowercase letter, a number and a symbol.
Write down your recovery code. It is shown only once and it is the safest way back in.
Also make a backup from the Protect tab. If you lose both, clearing app data is the only way in, and the backup restores your rules.

When your phone turns back on, this app starts protecting you again right away.
Without this, your phone would have no protection until you open the app and turn it on yourself.
You stay protected all the time, even right after a restart, without having to remember to turn it back on.
Keep this switched on so you are never left unprotected after a restart.
TacU-NS Firewall stores rules and logs on device only. No user account is required.
This tells you where your firewall data is kept.
All your rules and activity logs stay on your phone. Nothing is sent to a company server.
Some apps send your data to the internet to work. This app does not need to do that.
Your browsing history and app activity stay private, on your own device, at all times.
You do not need to sign up or log in to use this app.
If you uninstall the app, your logs are removed with it.

Uses Android VpnService for local traffic handling. Blocked domains are rejected on-device. Allowed DNS queries are forwarded to the DNS server set in Settings › DNS (by default Google Public DNS 8.8.8.8, or Cloudflare 1.1.1.1 if Google does not answer).
This explains why Android asks you to trust a \"VPN\" for this app.

Android only lets an app filter internet traffic without root access if it uses a VPN connection. This app uses that connection only on your phone — it does not send your traffic to a remote server like a normal VPN does.

Blocked websites are stopped right on your phone. Only the lookups needed to find a website are sent to the DNS server set in Settings › DNS (Google Public DNS 8.8.8.8 by default), so your phone knows where to connect.
You get ad and threat blocking without needing to root your phone, and without a company routing all your traffic through their servers.
The \"VPN\" icon you see in Android\'s status bar is normal and expected while this app is protecting you.
PDDL 1.0 — Public-domain IP-to-country data, built from internet registry and routing records

This app asks for %1$d permissions on your device. Here is exactly what each one is for — no permission is used for anything beyond what\'s listed below.

Needed to look up website addresses (DNS) and to download the block lists that power ad and threat blocking.
Lets the app tell whether you\'re on Wi-Fi or mobile data, so per-network blocking rules apply to the right connection.
Only used if you turn on \"Boot on Start\" — lets the firewall come back on automatically after your phone restarts.
See your list of installed apps
Needed to show the App Block list and let you choose which apps to block, by name and icon.

Android only allows an app to check your internet traffic — without root access — if it uses a VPN-style connection. This app\'s VPN runs entirely on your phone. It does not send your traffic to any outside server, the way a normal VPN service would.

Only one thing: when your phone looks up a website\'s address, that lookup is sent to the DNS server set in Settings › DNS so it can be resolved. By default that is Google Public DNS (8.8.8.8), and Cloudflare (1.1.1.1) only if Google does not answer. The content of your browsing, messages, or app data is never sent anywhere by this app.
Blocked sites never connect at all
When a website is on your block list, this app answers the look-up itself and says the website doesn\'t exist. Your phone never even attempts to connect to it.
No block list is enabled yet.

No account. No ads or analytics. Nothing is sold.

Website lookups are sent to the DNS server set in Settings › DNS (by default Google Public DNS 8.8.8.8, or Cloudflare 1.1.1.1 if Google does not answer) to find where sites are. Blocklists are downloaded from their public websites.

This app contains no analytics or advertising software, so nothing about your usage is measured or sold.

A blocklist is a list of known bad websites, made by security researchers and shared for free.
Turning one on stops your phone from connecting to every website on that list — mostly ads, trackers, and scam sites.
One list alone cannot catch everything. Using more than one list together catches more ads and threats.
Faster browsing with fewer ads, and less chance of accidentally visiting a harmful website.
